result.text:
## Why all of this sounds artificial
By now this probably sounds terribly artificial. Is anyone actually going to do scheduled check-ins, delayed cohabitation, conversations about hypothetical disasters, imagination exercises, not to mention resisting the heat of the moment stuff, and continuing your own reparenting practices when a warm body is available to do some of the soothing?
Well, you caught me. It is painfully artificial.
In a healthy communal society I don’t think most of this would even need a name. Other people would already know both of you. You’d have friends to go to, elders to ask, and people besides your partner who could help carry whatever was happening. Most of us don’t have much of that, so I end up recommending weird substitutes like scheduled check-ins.
If we ever build the communities I’m always going on about, maybe half of this advice can go in the trash.
---
## What doing it consciously looks like
Most of this I learned by getting it wrong. Some I figured out by thinking about it, and a few pieces I’m still trying out.
- Have the big conversations before making love. Don’t just ask what somebody’s values are. Ask what jealousy looks like for them, whether attraction to somebody else is speakable, what they do under stress, which old patterns are actually still current, how recent the healing is, what they want from you in a hard moment, and what they do with money. Concrete scenarios are better: if X happened, what would you want, and what would you probably do?
- Don’t let sex, cohabitation, and the rest of your life all accelerate together. If you can avoid moving in early, do. Housing can make that unrealistic, but living together gives you practical reasons to stay that have nothing to do with wanting to. Set a real date to ask how the relationship is going before there’s a crisis.
- Make deep friends together. Old friends will naturally be partial because they love one of you first. That’s fine. You still want some people around who actually know you both.
- Deciding “I want this person” is faster than deciding “I want to build my life with this person.” A wonderful lover can be a terrible co-parent, community member, or life partner. I also watch for “I’m taking a chance on this person” quietly becoming “this is the right person.” The second answer needs more evidence than the first.
- Keep your inner practices. Don’t let being loved become the reason you stop learning to love and regulate yourself.
- Pace the heavy conversations too. Ten profound talks in one weekend can feel deep before there’s much relationship underneath them. Play. Do ordinary things. Some information is better observed than extracted.
- And when something in you says, “Wait, slow down, something doesn’t fit,” don’t let early chemistry automatically overrule it. Ask what you need to ask.
---
# If you’re already in it
If you’re already married, raising children, living together, or ten years in, advice about slowing down before the relationship takes off is obviously late.
I wish I had a special method for that. I don’t. In all three of these relationships I learned the same annoying piece of common sense: one person can’t create mutual honesty. I could keep bringing up the problem, but I couldn’t make the other person look at it with me.
With Bee and Key, the biggest thing sitting underneath everything was trust. They wanted to be with me and would say they trusted me, but really they didn’t trust me, themself, or anyone else. It was all or nothing: blind trust, or none.
